learningObjective: Explain instruction selection as pattern-tiling of an IR tree against target-instruction templates.

canonicalClaims.claim: Instruction selection tiles an IR (tree or DAG) with target-instruction patterns, each carrying a cost; dynamic-programming or greedy algorithms find a minimum-cost cover, and multi-operation instructions like LEA or FMA can win by covering larger tiles.
conditions: Target ISA is expressible as a set of pattern rules with costs.
IR is in a form suitable for tiling (DAG or tree).
nonImplications: Does not imply DP tiling produces globally optimal machine code; interactions with scheduling and register allocation may impact final performance.
Does not imply pattern selection is the only approach; global instruction selection (GlobalISel) offers alternatives.

misconceptions.claim: Instruction selection is a synonym for register allocation.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Instruction selection chooses target opcodes; register allocation assigns storage. They are distinct backend passes.
Scheduling reorders instructions for pipeline efficiency; instruction selection chooses which instructions to emit.

misconceptions.claim: Multi-operation instructions like FMA always beat two separate instructions.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Precision semantics differ (FMA has one rounding vs two); some targets or code paths may prefer separate ops for numerical reasons or throughput reasons.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: IEEE 754 FMA spec; LLVM backend documentation

implementationFacts: LLVM SelectionDAG is a canonical pattern-based instruction selector.
LLVM GlobalISel provides an alternative pipeline (IRTranslator, Legalizer, RegBankSelect, InstructionSelect).
TableGen (.td files) describe target instruction patterns and costs.
performanceScenarios: x86 LEA can compute base + index*scale + disp in one instruction; targeting it well requires selectors to recognize the pattern in the IR.
